content.heading: 2.9 Dimension and Rank
content.paragraph: This section continues the discussion of subspaces and bases for subspaces, beginning with the concept of a coordinate system. The definition and example below should make a useful new term, dimension, seem quite natural, at least for subspaces of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$.﻿
content.heading: Coordinate Systems
content.paragraph: The main reason for selecting a basis for a subspace $H$, instead of merely a spanning set, is that each vector in $H$ can be written in only one way as a linear combination of the basis vectors. note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: Suppose the set $B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{p}\}$ is a basis for a subspace $H$. For each $\textbf{x}$ in $H\text{,}$ the coordinates of x relative to the basis B are the weights $c_{1},\ldots,c_{p}$ such that $\textbf{x} = c_{1}\textbf{b}_{1} + \cdots + c_{p}\textbf{b}_{p},$ and the vector in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$
is called the coordinate vector of x (relative to B ) or the $B\text{-coordinate}$vector of$\mathbf{x}$.1

content.paragraph: In general, if $B = \{\textbf{b}_{1},\ldots,\textbf{b}_{p}\}$ is a basis for $H$, then the mapping $\textbf{x}\mapsto\lbrack\textbf{x}\rbrack_{B}$ is a one-to-one correspondence that makes $H$ look and act the same as $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$ (even though the vectors in $H$ themselves may have more than $p$ entries). (Section 4.4 has more details.)
content.heading: The Dimension of a Subspace
content.paragraph: It can be shown that if a subspace $H$ has a basis of $p$ vectors, then every basis of $H$ must consist of exactly $p$ vectors. (See Exercises 35 and 36.) Thus the following definition makes sense.

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The dimension of a nonzero subspace $H$, denoted by $\text{dim~}H$, is the number of vectors in any basis for $H$ The dimension of the zero subspace $\{\textbf{0}\}$ is defined to be zero.2

content.paragraph: The space $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ has dimension $n$. Every basis for $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$ consists of $n$ vectors. A plane through $\textbf{0}$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{3}$ is two-dimensional, and a line through $\textbf{0}$ is one-dimensional.

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Recall that the null space of the matrix $A$ in Example 6 in Section 2.8 had a basis of $3$ vectors. So the dimension of $\text{Nul }A$ in this case is $3$. Observe how each basis vector corresponds to a free variable in the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$. Our construction always produces a basis in this way. So, to find the dimension of $\text{Nul }A$, simply identify and count the number of free variables in $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$.﻿

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: The rank of a matrix $A$, denoted by $\text{rank~}A$, is the dimension of the column space of $A$.﻿

content.paragraph: Since the pivot columns of $A$ form a basis for $\text{Col~}A$, the rank of $A$ is just the number of pivot columns in $A$.﻿

content.paragraph: The row reduction in Example 3 reveals that there are two free variables in $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$, because two of the five columns of $A$ are not pivot columns. (The nonpivot columns correspond to the free variables in $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$.) Since the number of pivot columns plus the number of nonpivot columns is exactly the number of columns, the dimensions of $\text{Col~}A$ and $\text{Nul }A$ have the following useful connection. (See the Rank Theorem in Section 4.6 for additional details.)

note.title: Theorem 14
note.heading: Theorem 14
The Rank Theorem
note.paragraph: If a matrix $A$ has $n$ columns, then $\text{rank~}A + \dim\text{Nul }A = n$.﻿

content.paragraph: The following theorem is important for applications and will be needed in Chapters 5 and 6. The theorem (proved in Section 4.5) is certainly plausible, if you think of a $p$-dimensional subspace as isomorphic to $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$. The Invertible Matrix Theorem shows that $p$ vectors in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$ are linearly independent if and only if they also span $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{p}$.﻿

note.title: Theorem 15
note.heading: Theorem 15
The Basis Theorem
note.paragraph: Let $H$ be a $p$-dimensional subspace of $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}\text{.}$ Any linearly independent set of exactly $p$ elements in $H$ is automatically a basis for $H\text{.}$ Also, any set of $p$ elements of $H$ that spans $H$ is automatically a basis for $H\text{.}$

content.heading: Rank and the Invertible Matrix Theorem
content.paragraph: The various vector space concepts associated with a matrix provide several more statements for the Invertible Matrix Theorem. They are presented below to follow the statements in the original theorem in Section 2.3.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
The Invertible Matrix Theorem (continued)
note.paragraph: Let $A$ be an $n \times n$ matrix. Then the following statements are each equivalent to the statement that $A$ is an invertible matrix.

list.item: The columns of A form a basis of ℝn.

content.heading: Proof
content.paragraph: Statement $(m)$ is logically equivalent to statements $(e)$ and $(h)$ regarding linear independence and spanning. The other four statements are linked to the earlier ones of the theorem by the following chain of almost trivial implications:

Statement $(g)$, which says that the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ has at least one solution for each $\textbf{b}$ in $\mathbf{\mathbb{R}}^{n}$, implies statement $(n)$, because $\text{Col\,\,}A$ is precisely the set of all $\textbf{b}$ such that the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{b}$ is consistent. The implications $(n)$ $\Rightarrow$ $(o)$ $\Rightarrow$ $(p)$ follow from the definitions of dimension and rank. If the rank of $A$ is $n\text{,}$ the number of columns of $A$, then $\text{dim~Nul }A = 0$, by the Rank Theorem, and so $\text{Nul }A = \{\textbf{0}\}$. Thus $(p)$ $\Rightarrow$ $(q)$. Also, statement $(q)$ implies that the equation $A\textbf{x} = \textbf{0}$ has only the trivial solution, which is statement $(d)$. Since statements $(d)$ and $(g)$ are already known to be equivalent to the statement that $A$ is invertible, the proof is complete.

note.title: Numerical Notes
note.heading: Numerical Notes
note.paragraph: Many algorithms discussed in this text are useful for understanding concepts and making simple computations by hand. However, the algorithms are often unsuitable for large-scale problems in real life.

Rank determination is a good example. It would seem easy to reduce a matrix to echelon form and count the pivots. But unless exact arithmetic is performed on a matrix whose entries are specified exactly, row operations can change the apparent rank of a matrix. For instance, if the value of $x$ in the matrix $\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 7 \\ 5 & x \end{bmatrix}$ is not stored exactly as $7$ in a computer, then the rank may be $1$ or $2$, depending on whether the computer treats $x - 7$ as zero.
In practical applications, the effective rank of a matrix $A$ is often determined from the singular value decomposition of $A\text{,}$ to be discussed in Section 7.4.
